articles.title: ‘Lauf’ and ‘minceur’: the words that made a 13-year-old from Melbourne a world Scrabble champion
articles.excerpt:
Dineth Fernando – who moved to Australia with his family in February – says he just needed to ‘find the word and play – that’s all’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Dineth...
articles.body_text:
Dineth Fernando – who moved to Australia with his family in February – says he just needed to ‘find the word and play – that’s all’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Dineth Fernando’s first language isn’t English and he only arrived in Melbourne six months ago – but already he’s claimed an international Scrabble title with an Australian flag draped around his shoulders.

The 13-year-old won the 2026 world youth Scrabble championships in the Kenyan capital of Nairobi over the weekend, becoming the third Australian representative in the competition’s history to take out the prize.

During the three-day tournament, Dineth played 24 games of the classic word game, going head-to-head against more than 130 opponents from 15 different countries.

“It took a lot of stress and effort to navigate through the days,” Dineth, who moved with his family in February from Sri Lanka, said.

“But I just needed to concentrate on the game, nothing else.

“Like, don’t care if there is a live camera going on, I just needed to jumble the rack, find the word and play – that’s all.”

This was Dineth’s third attempt at the world championships, and the trip to Nairobi had already forced him to contend with jetlag on top of the nerves.

But after more than 20 hours of play, and carefully placed words including “lauf” (a run in bobsleighing), “novelese” (a style of writing characteristic of poor novels), “minceur” (a French word for thinness), “histrio” (an archaic word meaning actor) and “postering”, the 13-year-old emerged victorious on Sunday.

Prasanna Fernando almost cried when his son was crowned the world youth Scrabble champion.

“I sometimes still can’t believe he actually won it because the level of competition was extremely high.

“But I always knew he was capable of doing it one day.”

Dineth got his first taste for the game when he and his family were still living in Sri Lanka.

At eight years old, he joined the school Scrabble club before hiring a private coach as he flew all over the country to compete.

His family moved to Australia in February for his father’s work, but he continued his pursuit for Scrabble greatness, entering competitions and playing against people like Melbourne-based two-time Scrabble world champion and 2006 youth Scrabble winner David Eldar, and even beating world champion finalist Harshan Lamabadusuriya.

His accolades quickly grew, becoming runner-up at the Wodonga open Scrabble championship, winning the Ballarat open championship and eventually taking out the Australian youth prize.

Scrabble Victoria secretary, Carol Johnsen, has faced the teenager a few times, and though he had luck on his side, she says he is also a force to be reckoned with.

“The tiles just flowed for him: he got the X and the Z and the Q and they all went in the right places.

“I had no hope, and he’s beat me by over 200 points each time.”

Dineth spends more than three hours a day studying Scrabble words and believes his discipline and hard work gave him an edge at the youth competition.

Though English is not his first language, he does not see this as an issue, since the game’s dictionary is a combination of many languages including English, Latin, French and more.

Nigel Richards, a five-time world champion became famous for winning Scrabble tournaments in languages he didn’t speak, taking out the French title in 2015 and 2018, and the Spanish-language competition in 2024.

For those at the top levels of Scrabble, it is closer to mathematics and pattern recognition than a language game, according to Johnsen.

But Dineth’s favourite thing about Scrabble is the opportunity it offers for him to learn new words.

After an almost 12,000km trip home, the 13-year-old returned to school on Thursday, where a hero’s welcome was waiting.

“It was a really great feeling that everyone – my friends and teachers – wished me,” he said.

He’s now got his eyes on the 2027 competition and is hoping to become the first youth champion to defend their title.

articles.title: UK defends seizing shadow fleet tanker after Putin threat
articles.excerpt:
Royal Marine Commandos were involved in the operation to seize the MT Smyrtos

The UK government has defended its seizure of a Russian "shadow fleet" oil tanker in the English Channel, after Russian P...
articles.body_text:
Royal Marine Commandos were involved in the operation to seize the MT Smyrtos

The UK government has defended its seizure of a Russian "shadow fleet" oil tanker in the English Channel, after Russian President Vladimir Putin threatened to "respond in kind".

The Smyrtos was taken to be anchored off Weymouth after Royal Marines Commandos intercepted and boarded it in a first-of-its-kind operation to disrupt the sanctioned tanker in June.

The vessel's captain, Ajay Pant, has been charged with breaching Russian sanctions, accused of directly or indirectly supplying or delivering prohibited Russian oil.

Overseeing Russian navy drills in the Pacific Ocean, Putin scolded Western countries for "seizing our vessels", branding such action "nothing other than piracy and banditry".

"If these plans are put into practice, we will have to respond in kind," Putin warned on Wednesday.

"And not necessarily in the waters where raids on our ships and vessels are planned, but wherever we deem it necessary and appropriate, anywhere."

Viktor Liina, commander of Russia's Pacific Fleet, accused Western countries such as Britain and France of operating their own "shadow fleets".

"We have the capacity to inspect and detain vessels of unfriendly states and their shadow fleets, and interagency cooperation is in place, ready to begin addressing these challenges," Liina said.

In response to Putin's comments, the UK government said Britain's armed forces and law-enforcement officers had boarded the Smyrtos "in full accordance with international law".

"The UK is disrupting and deterring shadow fleet vessels and their harmful maritime activity which is fuelling Russia's war with Ukraine," a government spokesperson said.

The spokesperson said unlike Russia's shadow fleet, "UK armed forces and commercial vessels operate firmly in line with international maritime law".

Watch: MoD footage shows commandos boarding and searching the tanker

Western nations allege Russia has been operating a "shadow fleet" to evade international sanctions imposed on its oil exports.

The UK Ministry of Defence says Russia has a fleet of more than 700 vessels, responsible for carrying 75% of the country's sanctioned oil.

This oil is a "critical lifeline for the Kremlin" in "sustaining Russia's illegal war", the MoD says.

Putin's comments come as the European Union intensifies pressure on Russia's shadow fleet.

In his remarks to Russian sailors, Putin singled out the EU, accusing member states of violating international maritime law and "attempting to restrict the movement of vessels belonging to our economic operators".

Many Western countries imposed sanctions on Russian energy following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Moscow has been accused of dodging them by shipping oil on aged tankers often with obscure ownership or insurance.

To combat this tactic, in 2024 the EU began sanctioning individual shadow fleet vessels – "Putin's dark fleet", as the European Council, the bloc's top group of national leaders, put it.

More than 630 vessels are sanctioned as of mid-August 2026, meaning they are banned from EU ports.

Meanwhile, several individual European countries have been seizing or detaining Russian-linked vessels or have carried out boardings or detentions when sanctions violations are suspected.

Most recently, the Italian navy, in conjunction with other EU countries, boarded a tanker in the central Mediterranean suspected of not being entitled to fly the flag it claimed.

Although that inspection did not result in a seizure of the vessel, others have.

Since the start of the year, nine shadow fleet tankers suspected of circumventing sanctions have been seized around the EU.

Royal Marines board Russian shadow fleet oil tanker in English Channel

What happened to Russian 'shadow fleet' tanker crew?

articles.title: South Korean airport becomes busiest in world for global traffic amid Iran war
articles.excerpt:
Incheon airport had 38.39m international passengers in first half of 2026, as traffic diverted from Middle East hubs

South Korea’s Incheon airport has become the world’s busiest airport for internati...
articles.body_text:
Incheon airport had 38.39m international passengers in first half of 2026, as traffic diverted from Middle East hubs

South Korea’s Incheon airport has become the world’s busiest airport for international passengers, in part owing to disruption in the Middle East caused by the Iran war.

The airport, South Korea’s main gateway, about 30 miles (48km) west of Seoul, handled 38.39 million international passengers in the first half of 2026, according to preliminary figures compiled by the Airports Council International (ACI), the global trade body for airports.

Heathrow in the UK was second, with 37.79 million, followed by Changi airport in Singapore with 34.53 million.

It is the first time Incheon has topped the international passenger rankings since opening in 2001. The airport was 10th in the world in 2002, rising to fifth in 2018 and third in 2024 and 2025.

Part of the increase was attributed to disruption caused by the US-Iran conflict, which weakened the role of Middle Eastern hubs such as Dubai and diverted some transfer traffic to alternative routes through east Asia, Incheon International Airport Corporation (IIAC) was quoted as saying by the Yonhap news agency.

Incheon’s international passenger traffic was up 6.3% year on year overall, with rising numbers of foreign visitors also contributing to the increase.

Foreigners accounted for 39.3% of Incheon’s passengers in the first half of the year, up from 35.2% for the whole of 2025. The proportion reached a record 44.4% in the second quarter, with IIAC attributing the increase largely to growing numbers of visitors from China and Japan, according to local media.

Heathrow, in west London, recorded 40 million passengers in total in the first half of the year, including both domestic and international travellers, its busiest first half on record. Passenger traffic to Asia-Pacific rose 7.9%, while capacity to the Middle East reportedly fell 16.5% owing to the regional conflict.

Earlier this week Istanbul overtook Heathrow as Europe’s busiest airport by total passenger numbers. Figures published on Tuesday showed 7.9 million passengers passed through Heathrow’s terminals in July, compared with Istanbul’s 8.15 million.

Incheon has also expanded its role as an international hub. It serves 101 airlines flying to 183 cities, including 158 international passenger destinations.

A four-phase expansion completed in late 2024 increased the airport’s annual capacity to 106 million passengers.

Kim Beom-ho, the acting president of IIAC, said the ranking reflected “the support of the government, the public’s encouragement and the hard work of everyone stationed at the airport”.

South Korea also lays claim to the world’s busiest air route. The domestic corridor between Gimpo airport and Jeju island had 14.4 million seats scheduled in 2025, according to the aviation data provider OAG, more than any other route in the world.

articles.title: FIFA’s Infantino backed by six Arab federations including Qatar and Morocco
articles.excerpt: Six ‌heads of Arab national football associations, including 2022 World Cup host Qatar and 2030 World ⁠Cup cohost Morocco, have joined the growing ⁠backing for FIFA President Gianni Infantino with foo...
articles.body_text:
Six ‌heads of Arab national football associations, including 2022 World Cup host Qatar and 2030 World ⁠Cup cohost Morocco, have joined the growing ⁠backing for FIFA President Gianni Infantino with football’s world governing body in crisis after a failed private investment plan.

Infantino, who ⁠is seeking re-election next year, has faced open revolt after three confederations – UEFA, AFC and CONCACAF – called for him to quit over his aborted ⁠bid to bring private investment into FIFA competitions, including the World Cup.

The Swiss administrator had proposed carving off the commercial rights to the World Cup and selling 20 percent to private investors to raise about $4.2bn.

“Recognising the important role of ‌Arab football in bringing people together and strengthening cooperation among football associations across the Arab world, we … express our full support for Mr Gianni Infantino, president of FIFA, and reaffirm our confidence in his leadership and continued commitment to the development of football worldwide,” the heads of the six federations said in a joint statement.

The statement was signed by ⁠the heads of the national federations of Qatar, ⁠Lebanon, Morocco, Sudan, Egypt and Mauritania. Four of the six signatories are also FIFA Council members.

“We deeply appreciate Mr Infantino’s sustained efforts to advance football globally, expand opportunities across all regions ⁠and strengthen the game’s role in bringing people and communities together,” they said.

“We look forward to continuing our ⁠close cooperation with him towards a stronger and ⁠more prosperous future for world football, expanding opportunities and further enhancing Arab football’s contribution to the global game.”

Infantino’s withdrawn proposal came with a $20m grant for member associations for the next ‌funding cycle, an amount that could have been doubled if they had signed the deal.

Despite the opposition of the three confederations in Europe, Asia, North and Central America and the Caribbean, which represent 136 of the ‌211 ‌member associations who will vote in the FIFA presidential election in March, Infantino still has plenty of allies in the game.

articles.excerpt: Rep. Pat Fallon unveiled legislation that would strip federal intelligence-related funding from colleges maintaining ties to Chinese Communist Party-linked groups, arguing it is necessary to protect s...
articles.body_text:
Rep. Pat Fallon unveiled legislation that would strip federal intelligence-related funding from colleges maintaining ties to Chinese Communist Party-linked groups, arguing it is necessary to protect sensitive U.S. research and national security.

FIRST ON FOX: Harvard allegedly failed to adequately safeguard research collaborations with Chinese institutions, including universities tied to Beijing’s military and defense-industrial base, according to a report from the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party.

Researchers affiliated with the New England Ivy League co-authored more than 140 publications with other researchers affiliated with a group of Chinese universities, according to the report reviewed by Fox News Digital ahead of its public release.

The "Seven Sons of National Defense" are a group of Chinese universities identified by the Pentagon and other U.S. officials as central to China’s defense research and military modernization efforts. The House Committee created to crackdown on China argues Harvard’s approach to research security opened the door for collaborations that could advance technological and military capabilities of the hostile nation.

Harvard also reported received more than $600 million from China under the federal Section 117 foreign-gift disclosure system — more than any other American university, according to the Education Department dashboard cited in the report. The committee argues the U.S. university's financial ties to China heighten the need for strict oversight of its research partnerships and foreign-funding disclosures.

Banners hanging from Memorial Church on the Harvard University campus in Cambridge, Massachusetts, US, on Tuesday, May 27, 2025. (Sophie Park/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

HARVARD TOPS NATION IN FOREIGN CASH HAUL AS COTTON DEMANDS PROBE INTO CHINA FUNDING

The stakes in the latest report extend far beyond Harvard. U.S. officials have warned for years that China uses academic partnerships and access to Western research to advance CCP strategic capabilities in military, surveillance and other areas.

The House Select Committee on China argues that universities receiving U.S. taxpayer funding must do more than meet the narrowest legal requirements when collaborating with institutions embedded in China’s military research system, particularly when it comes to technology with potential defense or military uses.

The report highlights a 2023 paper on bio-inspired soft robots for deep-sea exploration co-authored by a Harvard-affiliated researcher and a researcher from Beihang University, one of the Seven Sons institutions. Beihang, also known as Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, has appeared on the Commerce Department’s Entity List since 2001.

The committee report argues the work examined in the paper has potential military applications, including underwater detection, while Harvard’s research-compliance office characterized the project as nonmilitary research.

FOREIGN ROBOT BAN TARGETS CHINA OVER SECURITY FEARS

Harvard researchers also co-authored a 2023 paper with a researcher at China’s National University of Defense Technology, another institution on a U.S. restricted list, according to the report. That study involved magnetic materials and acknowledged partial support from the U.S. Army Research Office.

An image from a 2023 paper on bioinspired soft robots for deep-sea exploration co-authored by researchers affiliated with Harvard and China’s Beihang University. (House Select Committee on the CCP)

The committee said it reviewed publications spanning dozens of disciplines and found that engineering accounted for the largest share of Harvard-affiliated research involving Seven Sons institutions.

"From allowing violence against anti-China protestors to collaborating with entities linked to the PLA, Harvard has made serious mistakes and must act now to prevent more. It should use this investigation as a catalyst for significant reforms that end CCP influence on campus and prioritize secure American research," committee chairman Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., said in a statement.

The report also examines Harvard’s executive education program with China’s National Healthcare Security Administration, which trained Chinese health officials on international health-insurance systems.

According to the report, attendance and registration records show officials affiliated with the Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps, or XPCC, were listed in connection with some sessions. The Treasury Department sanctioned XPCC in 2020 over human-rights abuses against Uyghurs and other ethnic minorities in Xinjiang.

The report acknowledges it is unclear whether XPCC officials ultimately attended every program in question.

It alleges, however, that Harvard had advance participant information for a 2020 online session that included XPCC-affiliated officials and did not take further action.

Harvard professor Winnie Yip, who helped organize the executive education program, told committee investigators she did not know XPCC was a sanctioned entity at the time and had not received training on sanctions compliance, according to the report.

The report further alleges Harvard’s research-security practices focused too narrowly on technical legal compliance and failed to account for broader national-security risks posed by work with Chinese military-linked institutions.

It cites testimony from Harvard research official John H. Shaw, who said the university evaluates research collaborations case by case and does not prohibit all work involving robotics or Chinese institutions. The committee criticized that approach, arguing research with entities embedded in China’s military-civil fusion system can have military applications even when the research is unclassified and intended for publication.

Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, reviews the troops during his inspection of the Chinese People's Liberation Army PLA garrison stationed in the Macao Special Administrative Region, south China, Dec. 20, 2024. (Li Gang/Xinhua via Getty Images)

The report also raises questions about Harvard Global Research and Support Services, a nonprofit affiliated with the university that can accept awards when Harvard is unable to accept a sponsor’s terms directly. The committee alleges the entity could be used to circumvent federal foreign-gift reporting requirements, an allegation Harvard will likely dispute.

Harvard did not respond to Fox News’ request for comment on the House Committee report’s findings.

The report recommends that Harvard prohibit research relationships with entities on U.S. government restricted or sanctioned lists and centralize its research-security oversight. It also urges Congress to strengthen foreign-funding disclosure requirements for universities.

articles.title: MORNING GLORY: Democrat El-Sayed reminds us just one senator can do great damage to our military
articles.excerpt:
Fox News contributor Hugh Hewitt discusses far-left streamer Hasan Piker campaigning for Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed on ‘One Nation.’

It is not often that I write criticall...
articles.body_text:
Fox News contributor Hugh Hewitt discusses far-left streamer Hasan Piker campaigning for Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed on ‘One Nation.’

It is not often that I write critically of a Republican United States senator. But that happened in February 2023, when Alabama Sen. Tommy Tuberville placed a hold on military promotions to protest a Department of Defense policy that covered travel expenses for service members seeking reproductive healthcare across state lines. Tuberville's hold ultimately delayed the promotions of more than 400 senior military officers, many of whom were colonels or Navy captains awaiting promotion to general or flag rank, for roughly 10 months.

The "Tuberville Blockade" upended the lives and careers of hundreds of Army, Air Force and Marine Corps colonels and Navy captains by seriously disrupting carefully planned career paths and assignments. It also disrupted the carefully constructed career paths of the generals and admirals who were sidelined by the ill-considered embargo.

Career military officers ought never again to be held hostage for political goals. Sen. Tuberville eventually relented after months of mounting pressure from senators in both parties. He lifted his blanket "hold" after long meetings with his Senate colleagues, who emphasized to him that he was damaging the careers of people who had provided exemplary service over decades.

MORNING GLORY: MICHIGAN’S DEMOCRATIC SENATE PRIMARY HAD TWO WINNERS — BUT ONLY ONE WAS ON THE BALLOT

Sen. Tuberville is almost certainly going to be the next governor of Alabama, and hopefully he will be a better governor for having learned from his mistake. But the precedent he set in 2023 should alert everyone to why a radical leftist like Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed ought never to hold the office of United States senator.

U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville, R-Ala., speaks to reporters as he returns to his office at the U.S. Capitol on Feb. 10, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

El-Sayed is a sworn enemy of the State of Israel, and I fear that it is very unlikely that he will be a supporter of the American military. El-Sayed has also repeatedly appeared with controversial left-wing streamer Hasan Piker, including at campaign rallies. His staunch allegiance to Piker telegraphs exactly what he could do if he beats Republican Mike Rogers in the fall: wreak havoc on our military and Israel’s defenses. El-Sayed has already called for a complete embargo on weapons sales to Israel — even defensive weapons.

El-Sayed supports "the immediate and comprehensive enforcement of U.S. laws that condition the provision of military aid and sales." He argues this means "an immediate arms embargo on Israel," and El-Sayed specifically rejects the distinction between offensive and defensive weapons, meaning his position includes weapons such as Iron Dome interceptors, not merely offensive bombs and missiles.

This stance places him among the most outspoken Senate candidates opposing U.S. military support for Israel. As a true hater of Israel, would El-Sayed dust off the Tuberville playbook to try to bring aid to Israel to an end? There is no reason voters should assume he would hesitate to do so.  There’s a precedent, and it is easy to hear a Sen. El-Sayed arguing that he is just deploying the same tactic that a Republican senator used.

ABDUL EL-SAYED SAYS RALLYING WITH HASAN PIKER DOESN'T MEAN HE ENDORSES 'AMERICA DESERVED 9/11' REMARK

The question for Michigan voters is not whether one senator could single-handedly shut off every American weapon or dollar flowing to Israel. He could not. But Senator Tuberville’s 2023 blockade demonstrated how much disruption a determined senator can cause by exploiting the Senate’s rules and customary procedures to delay action and force political confrontations.

It is difficult to imagine El-Sayed losing sleep over the damage he would impose on the U.S. military. That’s the possibility Michigan voters have to consider when they cast ballots this fall.

President Donald Trump, center, and GOP Senate candidate former Rep. Mike Rogers, left, listen as Rep. John James, a Republican gubernatorial candidate, speaks at an event at the General Motors Proving Ground Monday, July 27, 2026, in Milford, Mich. (Paul Sancya/AP Photo)

There are a few pro-defense Democrats left, including Michigan’s own Elissa Slotkin. But just as GOP senators would not publicly criticize their colleague in 2023, the handful of Democrats who are serious about national security would likely adhere to the unwritten code of the Senate that prohibits public attacks on colleagues from their own party conference.

So the Michigan Senate race is the most important election in the country this year. The Republican volunteers willing to go to the battleground state and campaign for Rogers will be participating in a cause much bigger than themselves.

They will be protecting the country’s national security. El-Sayed isn’t simply an extremist. He’s a dangerous radical who should not be in a position to harm the country’s armed forces.

Hugh Hewitt is a Fox News contributor and host of "The Hugh Hewitt Show" heard weekday afternoons from 3 PM to 6 PM ET on the Salem Radio Network, and simulcast on Salem News Channel. Hugh drives Americans home on the East Coast and to lunch on the West Coast on over 400 affiliates nationwide, and on all the streaming platforms where SNC can be seen. He is a frequent guest on the Fox News Channel’s news roundtable, hosted by Bret Baier weekdays at 6pm ET. A son of Ohio and a graduate of Harvard College and the University of Michigan Law School, Hewitt has been a Professor of Law at Chapman University’s Fowler School of Law since 1996 where he teaches Constitutional Law. Hewitt launched his eponymous radio show from Los Angeles in 1990. Hewitt has frequently appeared on every major national news television network, hosted television shows for PBS and MSNBC, written for every major American paper, has authored a dozen books and moderated a score of Republican candidate debates, most recently the November 2023 Republican presidential debate in Miami and four Republican presidential debates in the 2015-16 cycle. Hewitt focuses his radio show and his column on the Constitution, national security, American politics and the Cleveland Browns and Guardians. Hewitt has interviewed tens of thousands of guests from Democrats Hillary Clinton and John Kerry to Republican Presidents George W. Bush and Donald Trump over his 40 years in broadcasting. This column previews the lead story that will drive his radio/ TV show today.

articles.title: Polls open in Clacton, where Farage spent more than £10,000 in byelection against Count Binface – UK politics live
articles.excerpt:
The Reform UK leader resigned as the MP for Clacton at the start of July and forced a byelection

Good morning. In the media, August is known as the “silly season”. With parliament not sitting and man...
articles.body_text:
The Reform UK leader resigned as the MP for Clacton at the start of July and forced a byelection

Good morning. In the media, August is known as the “silly season”. With parliament not sitting and many people on holiday, there is less proper news than normal, which means the nonsense stories get (even) more attention than usual. We are almost slap bang in the middle of the month, and today we’ve got a silly season classic in Clacton, where Nigel Farage, the Reform UK candidate, is fighting a byelection in which his main opponent is a joke candidate who dresses up as a dustbin.

Farage is not inherently silly. Few politicians have been more consequential over the past quarter of a century (because he did more than any other single individual to make the Brexit referendum happen); for most of the past 16 months his party has had a big poll lead and he has a very realistic chance of being the next PM; and even if he doesn’t become PM, his hard-right, anti-migrant, crass, crypto-friendly populism will have changed British politics significantly.

But this byelection is rather absurd because it is essentially pointless; all it will do is postpone, not resolve, the verdict on the financial sleaze allegations that Farage is facing (his alleged failure to properly declare donations, including a £5m gift from a cryptocurrency billionaire).

Voting started in Clacton about two hours ago.

Normally there is not much new to report on polling day. But Politico has published a good story by John Johnston and he reveals that Reform UK has spent more than £10,000 during the election campaign on social media adverts designed to help it see off the threat from Count Binface. Johnston says:

double quotation markPOLITICO analysis of the Reform UK leader’s digital campaign messages shows that Farage has run a twin-track strategy in the seaside seat as polls open Thursday. The two key themes of the digital air war have been painting Farage as a champion for local residents — as well as an insurgent leader harried by the “establishment” machine.

Farage and his party have spent more than £10,000 pushing those messages via ads on Meta’s platforms — which include Facebook and Instagram — in the campaign so far.

Johnston says Farage is the only candidate in the byelection using “paid Meta features to bolster his online campaign”. He says:

double quotation markAlmost £1,000 has been spent on videos of Farage urging local supporters to request the party deliver and install an “I’m with Nigel” garden sign. Meanwhile, around £500 went to ads asking voters to return their postal votes and “send a message to the establishment.”

The largest single sum — between £4,000-£4,500 — was spent on an almost five-minute campaign video in which Farage waxes lyrical about the connection he’s made with local constituents, while claiming his party’s surging success has resulted in the powers-that-be using “foul means” to hamper him.

“Rather than being judged by the political class and the mainstream media, I am going to let you, the voters in the Clacton constituency, make a decision,” he said. “I want you to be my judge, not the political elite.”

There is not much else happening in Westminster politics. But it is a big day for A-level students, with results out this morning. Tom Ambrose is covering that on a separate live blog.

As I explained last month, we are no longer going to have comments open below the line on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints. There is a longer post here about how we hope this will work.

articles.title: New Mississippi law expands death penalty to include inmates on child sexual battery convictions
articles.excerpt:
James Duckett was recently executed for the 1987 rape and murder of 11-year-old Tereasa McAbee. Investigators believe he also Jeanifer Weldon that same year. (Credit: WTVT)

A new Mississippi law adde...
articles.body_text:
James Duckett was recently executed for the 1987 rape and murder of 11-year-old Tereasa McAbee. Investigators believe he also Jeanifer Weldon that same year. (Credit: WTVT)

A new Mississippi law added sexual battery of a child under 12 to the list of crimes eligible for the death penalty.

Senate Bill 2821, which took effect July 1, creates the crime of "capital sexual battery" and allows prosecutors to seek the death penalty against defendants 18 or older in qualifying cases involving victims younger than 12.

If a defendant is convicted, the jury must unanimously find at least two specific aggravating factors beyond a reasonable doubt before the defendant is eligible for the death penalty. At least 8 of the 12 jurors must then recommend death. But if the death penalty is not recommended by jurors, the mandatory sentence would be life in prison without parole.

ACCUSED CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSIN TYLER ROBINSON ASKS JUDGE TO TAKE POTENTIAL DEATH PENALTY OFF TABLE

A new Mississippi law added sexual battery of a child under 12 to the list of crimes eligible for the death penalty.

State Sen. Jeremy England, the bill's author, said the legislation seeks to give the worst punishment for crimes against the state's most vulnerable population.

"That is a crime that, I think, shocks the conscience, certainly. Those are the worst types of crimes against the most innocent of our citizens here in Mississippi," England said, according to WLBT.

But critics question whether capital punishment serves as a deterrent to crimes against young victims or if it could lead to children becoming too afraid to come forward knowing that doing so may end someone's life.

The law marks a shift from previous state policy restricting capital punishment to inmates convicted on murder charges. (The Promise of Justice Initiative via AP)

Abraham Bonowitz, executive director of Death Penalty Action, told the outlet he once supported the death penalty but changed his position, arguing that executions are unnecessary when a life sentence keeps an inmate permanently behind bars.

"There is no need for executions when we can throw away the key," Bonowitz said.

TWO FLORIDA INMATES DIE IN RARE DOUBLE EXECUTION AFTER SCOTUS DENIES STAYS

Senate Bill 2821 took effect on July 1. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

Bonowitz also said extending the death penalty to child sexual assault cases could deter victims from alerting authorities of the abuse they endured.

"Most of those kinds of crimes are by people that the child knows and you’re asking a child to then testify against a relative and try to get them executed," he said.

articles.title: Met police incapable of change, says mother of murdered sisters after Simon Levy case
articles.excerpt:
Mina Smallman, whose daughters were killed in north London park in 2020, says force ‘decides who matters’

The Metropolitan police does not take all cases of violence against women seriously and inste...
articles.body_text:
Mina Smallman, whose daughters were killed in north London park in 2020, says force ‘decides who matters’

The Metropolitan police does not take all cases of violence against women seriously and instead “decides who matters”, the mother of two murdered women has said.

Mina Smallman, whose daughters Bibaa Henry and Nicole Smallman were killed in a north London park in 2020, also said Britain’s biggest police force was incapable of change. Two police officers were jailed in 2021 after taking photographs of the dead bodies of her daughters and sharing the images in WhatsApp groups, referring to them as “dead birds”.

Commenting on the case of the sex offender Simon Levy, 40, who was left free to kill two women after police failings, she said: “One of the women that were murdered, because she was a sex worker, she wasn’t taken seriously. They didn’t look into her murder until he murdered a mother of four, and then they joined the two cases together.

“How ridiculous is that. Once again, the Met is deciding who matters. Both those women’s lives were important to their families, how dare they decide that they weren’t going to look into that case.”

Levy, who this week was given a whole-life sentence for his crimes, was also convicted earlier this year of sexually assaulting 11 other women, 10 of them on trains and the underground in London between 2023 and 2025.

Smallman said she had been in contact with the head of the Metropolitan police, Sir Mark Rowley, after reading about the case. She told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “After reading this case I sent a text message to Sir Mark and said: ‘How many times are you going to stand up publicly and apologise for failures in the Met?’

“It becomes a joke. The truth is, the Metropolitan police is too big for any senior team to be able to have a hands-on understanding of the day-to-day activities of that organisation.”

She said the Met was incapable of change because it was “too big”. “I believe that Sir Mark Rowley wants to change the Met and wants to do things differently, but they haven’t got a clue.”

She added: “We are asking them to do too much, they haven’t got the finances, it has become riddled with inactivity, corruption, misogyny, racism, and they just can’t do it.”

The crime and policing minister Sarah Jones previously described Levy as a monster and said the failings that had allowed him to remain free were “deeply concerning”.

Jones signalled the government would allow the relevant institutions and police watchdog to establish what had gone wrong. “The fact that Levy was able to inflict such devastating harm after being freed by police and the courts is deeply concerning,” she said. “It raises serious questions that require urgent answers.”

Rowley denied that the Met had not done enough, saying: “The inference that the Met didn’t try on this death is not true, the Met tried.”

But he said he did not understand why the Prison Service released Simon Levy after he sexually assaulted one of its staff members in jail.

Levy was questioned by police about the assault five months after his release, which Rowley said was “too slow”.

He told the Today programme: “That’s one of the things we’ve apologised for, but of course there are two mistakes in that: you’ve got he was released on licence by the Prison Service, having sexually assaulted in prison one of its people, I don’t understand that decision either.

“I’m prepared to come here and be accountable, we’ve got two officers being referred to be investigated by the independent office of police complaints, we take our accountability seriously.

“The rest of the system is not doing that. The Prison Service should not have released somebody who’s indecently assaulting its staff.”

articles.title: How to stay safe during an earthquake: A visual guide
articles.excerpt:
When an earthquake happens and the ground starts moving, what you do next can make a big difference to your safety.

This visual guide lays out five practical steps, from making your home more earthqu...
articles.body_text:
When an earthquake happens and the ground starts moving, what you do next can make a big difference to your safety.

This visual guide lays out five practical steps, from making your home more earthquake-safe and preparing an emergency survival kit to protecting yourself during the shaking and after it stops.

Earthquake safety starts before the ground begins to move. Look around your home, workplace or school and identify things that could fall, break or become dangerous during strong shaking.

Secure tall furniture such as bookcases and cabinets to walls and place heavy or breakable objects on lower shelves. Secure televisions and other large objects that could fall.

Learn how to safely shut off gas, electricity and water, and know where the main controls are. Stay away from windows, glass and other objects that could fall.

Having an emergency kit somewhere that is easy to reach is always a good idea. After an earthquake, power, water and communications may be disrupted. Having essential supplies ready means you do not have to search for them in the middle of an emergency.

Your emergency kit should include: Drinking water, non-perishable food, a first-aid kit, a flashlight, extra batteries, a battery-powered or hand-crank radio, a whistle and essential medicines.

Also include a power bank, copies of important documents, some cash and sturdy shoes to protect your feet from broken glass and debris.

If you are indoors when the earthquake begins, stay inside and protect yourself until the shaking stops.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) advises that you should not run outside while the building is shaking. Falling glass, debris, and other objects can make the area especially dangerous, so you are less likely to be injured if you stay where you are.

There is no single response that fits every situation. Your surroundings determine the hazards you need to avoid.

First, check yourself and others for injuries. Then look for hazards around you.

The end of the shaking does not necessarily mean the danger is over. Aftershocks can follow, and earthquakes can leave behind fires, gas leaks, damaged buildings, broken glass and downed power lines.

If you suspect a gas leak because of a damaged pipe or the smell of gas, leave the area. Do not attempt to turn the gas back on yourself. If electrical wiring is damaged, avoid touching it and follow local guidance about shutting off power.

Be prepared for aftershocks. If shaking starts again, Drop, Cover and Hold On.

Use your phone carefully after an earthquake. Avoid unnecessary calls to prevent overloading phone networks. Use text messages or data services when possible, and keep your phone available for emergency communication and official updates. Save battery power by reducing screen brightness, closing unnecessary apps and using a power bank if available.

After an earthquake, stay alert, follow official information and help others when it is safe to do so. The right preparation and a calm response can make a critical difference.

articles.title: Pentagon official and former Aukus sceptic says deal is ‘full steam ahead’, echoing Trump
articles.excerpt:
Elbridge Colby, a US under secretary of war, says he is ‘very pleased’ with the nuclear submarine program’s progress

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Elbridge Colby, the t...
articles.body_text:
Elbridge Colby, a US under secretary of war, says he is ‘very pleased’ with the nuclear submarine program’s progress

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Elbridge Colby, the third-highest-ranking official at the Pentagon and formerly an avowed Aukus sceptic, has mirrored his president’s language on the nuclear submarine deal, saying it is “full steam ahead”.

Colby, a US under secretary of war, was the author of the Trump administration’s review of the Aukus deal, which would see the US sell three in-service Virginia-class submarines to Australia, before the development of Australia’s domestically built Aukus-class submarines.

The original draft of Colby’s review was understood to be sceptical about the Aukus agreement’s prospects of success, but was rewritten – on some accounts twice – to more closely align with the president’s position that Aukus was “full steam ahead”.

Colby told an Asia-Pacific press briefing on Thursday “we’re very pleased to say that Aukus is – as the president said – full steam ahead”.

He said the Pentagon was “very pleased with the progress that has been made since the conclusion of the Aukus review which … has provided a roadmap for the success of the Aukus program.

“We all know this is an historic endeavour on the part of both countries, but particularly for Australia.”

The first Virginia-class submarine is slated to be sold to Australia in 2032.

“We remain optimistic but also clear-eyed about what we all need to do,” Colby said. “We will just keep knocking down the targets on our side. We have every expectation the Australian side will do the same.”

He said the US had “no better ally” than Australia, and that the US and Australia enjoyed a “deep alignment of thinking”.

“Australia really sees things through the lens of collective defence and a strategy of deterrence by denial designed to sustain a balance of power in this key region.”

Colby was asked about production rates of Virginia-class submarines, and also the potential presence of nuclear-armed submarines at Australian ports.

US boat-building rates have remained stubbornly laggard. It is currently manufacturing Virginia-class submarines at a rate of 1.1 to 1.2 a year.

That rate needs to be lifted to two boats a year to service US needs alone, and 2.33 boats a year in order to sell any to Australia.

Pillar one of the Australia-UK-US (Aukus) agreement involves Australia being given the technology to command its own fleet of conventionally armed, nuclear-powered submarines. There are two stages:

• First, Australia will buy between three and five Virginia-class nuclear-powered submarines from the US, the first of these in 2032. But before any boat can be sold to Australia, the US commander-in-chief – the president of the day – must certify that the US relinquishing a submarine will not diminish its navy’s undersea capability. The US submarine fleet now has only three-quarters of the submarines it needs (49 boats of a force-level goal of 66). And there are significant concerns the US cannot build enough submarines for its own needs, let alone any for Australia.

• Second, by the “late 2030s”, according to the "optimal pathway" outlined in Australia’s submarine industry strategy, the UK will launch the first specifically designed and built Aukus submarine for Britain’s Royal Navy.

The first Australian-built Aukus submarine, for the Royal Australian Navy, will be in the water “in the early 2040s”. Australia will build up to eight Aukus boats, with the final vessels launched in the 2060s.

Each of Australia’s nuclear submarines is forecast to have a working life of about three decades. Australia will be responsible for securing and storing the nuclear waste from its submarines - including high-level nuclear waste and spent fuel (a weapons proliferation risk) - for thousands of years.

Aukus is forecast to cost Australia up to A$368bn to the mid-2050s.

Colby said the Pentagon was “very focused on submarine production, submarine maintenance, and making sure that that’s in as strong a place as it can be”.

He said the Pentagon and broader Trump administration had “a very clear understanding” with Australia about its expectations under the Aukus agreement.

“They know what is required, we’ve been very clear in private with them.

“[Those discussions were] designed to give everybody a reasonable, stable and realistic set of expectations to achieve this historic ambition that will put us all in a stronger place.”

Colby did not comment on the potential of nuclear-armed US submarines docking at Australian ports.

The US maintains a policy of “strategic ambiguity” around its nuclear capabilities, refusing to confirm or deny whether its nuclear-capable platforms – including aircraft submarines – are carrying nuclear warheads.

The Australian Department of Defence says it respects the US policy and does not ask whether platforms – such as B-52 bombers landing on Australian soil – are nuclear-armed.

Colby’s comments came in the same week an inquiry into Aukus held public hearings in Sydney, Newcastle and Port Kembla.

The former prime minister Malcolm Turnbull told the inquiry Australia’s blind faith in the Aukus submarine deal was “stark staring bonkers”, and argued the asymmetric deal with the US would likely result in no submarines at all for Australia.

Giving evidence to the inquiry in Sydney, Turnbull said the US was prevented by its own legislation from selling any submarines to Australia if that would “degrade” its own fleet.

articles.title: Europe heatwave live: Temperatures of 40C expected in Spain, with amber heat health warning in place across large parts of UK
articles.excerpt:
In France, 80 departments have been placed on an orange heat warning

With record dry conditions in July and a dry start to August, nearly three-quarters of England and the whole of Wales are in droug...
articles.body_text:
In France, 80 departments have been placed on an orange heat warning

With record dry conditions in July and a dry start to August, nearly three-quarters of England and the whole of Wales are in drought, heaping pressure on water resources for households, agriculture and the environment, PA reported.

And England and Wales have already seen as many wildfires this year as in the whole of 2025.

Some 1,017 wildfires have been recorded in England and Wales this year, according to data shared by the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC), the same as last year’s record-breaking total, PA said.

Over in England, the amber warning by the Met Office stretches from London to Sheffield, covering parts of the South East, East Midlands, East of England, West Midlands and South Yorkshire and is in place from 9am to midnight on Thursday, PA reported.

“Temperatures [in areas covered by the amber warning] could reach highs of around 36, 37, possibly 38C.

Now when you get these sorts of high temperatures, well that’s when we could see impacts to our infrastructure, our railway lines, our roads, they are not designed for this sort of heat.

And more people are likely to be impacted by how hot it is with regards to their health.

It could be the hottest day of the year so far if we get above 38C, and if we get above 38.5C, well it could be the hottest August day on record, but that’s actually pretty unlikely.”

PA noted that the UK is facing increasingly extreme conditions such as heatwaves, drought and wildfires fuelled by climate change, which is mostly driven by greenhouse gas emissions from burning fossil fuels for power plants, vehicles, heating and industry.

Romania began the complete shutdown of its only nuclear plant after water levels in the Danube, used to cool the site, fell to a record low, the national nuclear energy company said.

Nuclearelectrica already shut down last month one of the two reactors at the Cernavoda power plant, which usually generates a fifth of the Eastern European country’s total electricity, AFP reported.

The second needed to shut as well “due to the significant and ongoing drop in the water level of the River Danube”, it said in a statement.

This is despite several measures taken to avert a complete shutdown, including blowing up a rock and sinking four barges filled with rocks to divert its flows.

The government will look at banning disposable barbecues as wildfires continue to rage across the UK, Andy Burnham has said.

Disposable barbecues have been the cause of a number of serious fires over the last few years, but campaigners were critical of the prime minister’s failure to link those fires more broadly to the climate crisis.

Disposable barbecues, which can be carried into public areas, present a number of problems: they remain hot, sometimes for hours, after they are used, making them extremely difficult to dispose of safely, and when they cannot be carried away, people are forced to leave them or place them into bins where they carry on smouldering.

Burying the barbecues, as some try to do, will not stop the danger as these trays of charcoal can reach 450C and will carry on burning underground, where they can still ignite fires long after use. On beaches, the buried coals and metal grills are also a hazard for walkers, and in fields for farm animals.

Over the last few years they have been identified as the cause of a number of serious fires including:

Macclesfield, Cheshire, July 2026: a large woodland fire that was tackled by dozens of firefighters. Cheshire fire and rescue service said a discarded barbecue was the probable cause

Three separate fires in one day around London, July 2026: in Feltham, 6 hectares of heathland close to houses were damaged. The London fire brigade urged people not to use disposable barbecues and to properly extinguish cigarettes after crews tackled three grass fires.

The Trossachs, Scotland, May 2025: covered 2 hectares in the Glen Finglas region of the national park. Glen Finglas is the biggest Woodland Trust site in the UK. The barbecue understood to have sparked that fire was found with a burger still on the grill.

Straight off the back of the solar eclipse last night, we’re heading into a solar inferno as extreme heat returns today, with temperatures above 40C in parts of Spain and up to 38C in London and Paris.

An amber weather warning for extreme heat is in place across large parts of the UK, while 80 French departments have been placed on an orange heat warning.

Drink lots of water, stay cool and look after your vulnerable family members, kids and pets. And keep reading Europe Live, obviously.

I will bring you all the updates from the UK and across the continent here.

It’s Thursday, 13 August 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

articles.title: As temperatures soar, ‘exceptionally serious’ drought imperils UK farmers
articles.excerpt:
Cambridgeshire, United Kingdom – Tom Pearson looks down at a crack in his own field, wide enough to plunge his fingers into.

Beneath the stubble of a freshly combined oat crop on his Manor Farm in Ca...
articles.body_text:
Cambridgeshire, United Kingdom – Tom Pearson looks down at a crack in his own field, wide enough to plunge his fingers into.

Beneath the stubble of a freshly combined oat crop on his Manor Farm in Caxton, near Cambridge, the ground has split, the soil having lost so much moisture that it has torn apart. A cover crop planted to shield the ground beneath the oats never really established before the early heat of this growing season arrived.

“It makes you wonder if it’s worth it,” Pearson said, looking out over the land his family has held since the 1680s. He then reconsiders. The cracks could have been worse – as in, he could have pushed his hand and forearm into them – if he had not spent the past 11 years trying to build resilience into this soil.

No one is happy about this growing season in the United Kingdom and across Europe – neither the conventional farmers watching their yields collapse nor those who have spent a decade trying to prepare for exactly this scenario.

Almost three-quarters of land in England is currently in drought after record-low rainfall and unusually high temperatures.

As the fifth heatwave of the summer arrives, England and Wales have recorded their driest July since records began in 1836.

Large stretches of the country have seen barely a 10th of the rain they would expect in an average month. For farmers, the consequences are hard to ignore.

“The fact that we’ve harvested more than half the winter wheat crop before the end of July reflects the challenging growing season many arable farmers have experienced,” said Jamie Burrows, chair of the National Farmers’ Union’s Combinable Crops Board.

He said the industry urgently needs government investment in crop varieties bred for drought and disease resistance, alongside a planning system that makes it easier to build on-farm water storage.

This is not an isolated year. It is the third drought in five years and the second in a row – a pattern the National Drought Group’s chair, Helen Wakeham, has called “an exceptionally serious situation” with “long-lasting impacts”.

He trained as a doctor in Edinburgh, worked in the NHS, and spent time in humanitarian aid work overseas before returning to his family’s land in 2015 with no formal agricultural training.

What he brought instead was a habit of testing evidence rather than assumptions.

He moved towards regenerative methods, including no-till farming and sharply reduced chemical inputs – and this year, into small plots of ancient grain varieties sourced from seed banks in the United States, Poland, the Czech Republic and the John Innes Centre in Norwich.

“They’ve got deep roots, they’re used to growing in drier situations,” he said. “It’s probably the perfect year for them.”

Einkorn and emmer are among the earliest wheat species domesticated by humans about 10,000 years ago in the Fertile Crescent of what today would be parts of Iraq, Syria and southeastern Turkiye.

They were domesticated thousands of years before modern fertilisers and intensive agricultural systems, as their wild ancestors evolved under water-limited conditions.

But the rest of Pearson’s farm tells a more complicated story.

His yields are down for a third consecutive year. Even with the marginal benefits of reduced tillage – using half the diesel of a conventional farm – it has not been enough to offset three years of poor harvests.

“We know we’re doing the right thing,” he said. “We’re measuring it, we’re moving forwards from a carbon and soil biology point of view … but we’re still being hit quite badly with these extreme weather events.”

Farmers went into this growing season already exposed.

Fuel and fertiliser prices surged this spring after United States and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February closed the Strait of Hormuz to shipping, disrupting global energy and fertiliser markets.

Drought then arrived shortly after seeding.

The regenerative farming Pearson has championed is often presented as one way of improving resilience to climate stress and the uncertainty of global energy markets.

The argument is that healthier soils can retain more water, while lower input costs – less fuel, fertiliser and chemical sprays – can partly offset the potential of lower yields.

“We’ve absolutely bought into the fact that we’re nature-friendly farmers,” he said. “But we’re taking fairly epic hits on our profits because we’re making change, and that’s risk in business.”

Even the best-managed soil has its limits.

“We’re talking about an extreme weather event that even the best soils might not survive with,” he said.

The scale of the challenge goes well beyond Pearson’s fields in the UK.

Rowan Douglas, an insurance risk specialist and former head of Howden’s Climate Risk and Resilience team, led a study published in May 2025 by the European Investment Bank and European Commission modelling agricultural climate risk across the European Union.

The research found that extreme-weather losses already average 28 billion euros ($32bn) a year across the bloc, rising to 40 billion euros ($46bn) by 2050. In a bad year, that figure could reach 60 billion euros ($70bn) now, or 100 billion euros ($115bn) by mid-century, with yields down by a fifth across the EU.

Roughly 80 percent of that risk is currently uninsured, borne directly by farmers. The UK, outside the EU and outside that study, has no comprehensive national crop-insurance scheme for farmers.

Pearson’s own ask of the government is less about subsidy levels than about knowledge.

He supports the shift towards paying farmers for public goods like soil health, but argues the industry is still “a bit short on the knowledge, a bit short on the data” – particularly on nutritional benefits and which varieties can realistically withstand these conditions.

Douglas, the risk specialist, argued the most useful first step is to properly quantify the financial risk the nation is already facing, the way his team did for the rest of the EU.

“Britain could do it better than anyone else because we’ve got better data and great institutions,” he said, meaning the underlying capacity to do this work well, even if the work itself is still outstanding.

The harder question, in his view, is how fairly to share the growing burden of risk between farmers and everyone who benefits from what they grow.

Back in his field, Pearson gestures towards a cluster of new housing across the road from his farm.

The local town is creeping closer, and he has started treating that proximity as an asset rather than a threat.

He talks about peri-urban farming so a portion of what he grows can reach nearby tables directly. It is a small step, but it points to something larger – helping people understand what they eat, where it comes from, and how a changing climate is now shaping both.

articles.title: How to keep babies and children safe in heatwaves
articles.excerpt:
Biological factors mean a child’s core temperature rises faster than an adult’s – and that can result in a medical emergency

Children and babies are more vulnerable in heatwaves than healthy adults. ...
articles.body_text:
Biological factors mean a child’s core temperature rises faster than an adult’s – and that can result in a medical emergency

Children and babies are more vulnerable in heatwaves than healthy adults. As temperatures rise again, how do we keep children safe?

The biological systems that regulate heat in the human body are controlled by a region of the brain called the hypothalamus. It is the body’s master thermostat, acting to keep our internal temperature around 37C. It also detects when we need more fluids.

When the hypothalamus detects a rise in temperature, it initiates responses such as sweating, which cools the body through evaporation, or vasodilation, which directs warm blood to vessels near the surface of the skin, where heat can radiate away.

But in children, particularly those under the age of five, the hypothalamus is not fully developed. They sweat less and do not realise when they are thirsty.

Also, children’s smaller physical size gives them a substantially greater body surface area-to-mass ratio than adults, meaning they absorb heat faster. They are also more likely to be physically active, and less likely to pace themselves, giving them much higher rates of metabolic heat production compared with adults.

All these factors mean children’s core temperatures rise faster, and stay high, compared with an adult.

If a child has been out too long in the sun, they may begin to develop heat exhaustion. They may sweat excessively, their skin may appear pale and clammy, and they may become dizzy, irritable or intensely thirsty. In more serious cases, they may begin to suffer muscle cramps and nausea, or even start vomiting.

At this point it is important to act, encouraging your child to come to a cooler, shaded spot, to have cold drinks, and to cool them down with wet towels or water, because the next stage – heatstroke – is even more severe.

According to the British Red Cross, heatstroke occurs when someone becomes so hot their brain’s thermostat fails. A child with heatstroke may have hot, flushed and dry skin, a headache, worsening confusion and restlessness, and a body temperature of more than 40C. He or she may lose consciousness. It is a medical emergency.

Overheating carries particularly serious health risks for children under five, and it is especially dangerous for babies, increasing the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (Sids).

During the June heatwave in the UK, one in six babies were living in overheated homes, according to research by housing activists. Some parents were going as far as booking air-conditioned hotel rooms to keep their children cool.

“Things to think about when it comes to children in heatwaves include: ensuring children stay well-hydrated; encouraging rest in cool, shaded areas; dressing children in light, loose-fitting clothing; and monitoring for signs of heat distress, such as fatigue, dizziness, or nausea,” said Dr Jessica Mee, an expert in heat physiology at the University of Worcester.

Babies, in particular, need special treatment, since they are so reliant on adults to make adaptations for them. In very hot weather, they may need extra breast or bottle feeds. They should not be left to sleep in their pram, which can become hot and airless, and when they are put down to sleep, parents should ensure there is good air circulation around them.

If you have a newborn, the National Health Service recommends keeping their room at a temperature of between about 16C and 20C.

If you are using a fan, do not point it directly at your baby, but use it to keep the air circulating around them. If you do not have a fan, and it is really hot, you can put cool, damp cloths on your baby’s body – but check on them regularly to ensure they are not getting too cold.

articles.title: Three US states to hold executions on same day for first time since 2010
articles.excerpt:
Tennessee, Alabama and Oklahoma are set to execute inmates via lethal injection in what would be the first time since 2010 that three people are put to death on the same day in the United States.

The...
articles.body_text:
Tennessee, Alabama and Oklahoma are set to execute inmates via lethal injection in what would be the first time since 2010 that three people are put to death on the same day in the United States.

The three inmates, who were all sentenced to death for murders, are scheduled to be put to death on Thursday.

In Tennessee, Anthony Darrell Hines will be executed for the 1985 murder of Catherine Jean Jenkins, a 54-year-old woman working as a motel maid in Kingston Springs. He was sentenced to death the following year, and despite winning a new sentencing hearing, was again sentenced to death in 1989.

Alabama is set to give 42-year-old Jeremy Williams the lethal injection for the 2021 rape and murder of five-year-old Kamarie Holland. Williams raped and strangled Holland after offering her mother $2,500 for the girl to perform a sex act, prosecutors said. Williams pleaded guilty to the charges, declined to appeal and asked for his death sentence to be carried out.

“To see on video what he did to this baby, what a grown man could do to a child, it’s shocking, it’s horrible, it’s disgusting,” Russell County District Attorney Richard Chancey said. “It’s just a level of evil.”

In Oklahoma, 70-year-old Carlos Cuesta-Rodriguez will also be executed for fatally shooting his girlfriend Olimpia Fisher in 2003. He would be the third person put to death this year in Oklahoma and the 20th under Republican Governor Kevin Stitt.

Eleven states carried out executions in 2025. If the Tennessee and Alabama lethal injections take place, six states will have had executions in 2026.

The executions are taking place amid a steady decline in support for the death penalty in the US.

The last three executions on the same day happened 16 years ago, in Louisiana, Ohio and Texas.

About 52 percent of Americans say the death penalty is morally acceptable, the lowest number since the 1970s, a poll by Gallup revealed.

articles.title: More troops to be sent to West Bank village besieged by Israeli settlers
articles.excerpt:
The Israeli army pictured in the West Bank village of Qusra on Wednesday

The Israeli military says it will deploy additional troops to the occupied West Bank after failing to force away Israeli settl...
articles.body_text:
The Israeli army pictured in the West Bank village of Qusra on Wednesday

The Israeli military says it will deploy additional troops to the occupied West Bank after failing to force away Israeli settlers who have trapped two Palestinian families in their homes since Sunday.

The Abu Ridi and Hassan families - who live on the outskirts of the village of Qusra, south of Nablus - made appeals for help after their water and power supplies were cut off and their food stocks ran low.

The case is the latest to draw attention to the relative impunity of settlers and how Israeli forces are struggling to deal with rising settler violence.

Videos shared from Qusra overnight show a dozen Israeli security vehicles – including a bulldozer.

In later footage – filmed in the daylight – there is a long line of Israeli security forces on the road to the Palestinian village, which remains a closed military zone.

Local media reports say that a nearby Israeli settler outpost was demolished.

Qusay Abu Ridi, who has been trapped by settlers in his home since Sunday with his water and power cut off, told the BBC that the house had been attacked again overnight and that a few settlers remained in the area, hiding from the army.

His brother – who owns the property – is a Palestinian-American businessman who had complained to the US embassy.

The US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee said his embassy had asked Israel to remove the settlers, describing them as "Israeli terrorists".

"Actions by those who carried out this horrific act of terror meant to intimidate and harass this family are disgusting. No excuse for such thuggish behavior," he posted on X.

Watch: How Israeli settlers are besieging Palestinian family homes in West Bank

The situation in Qusra first began on Sunday when settlers blocked the road to the Palestinian families' gates and cut off their power and water supplies. The first Israeli soldiers who came to the site prayed with the settlers – an act for which the Israel military later said they would be disciplined.

On Wednesday an attempt by Israeli security forces to dislodge the settlers led to confrontations with a bigger group – and ultimately failed.

Palestinian security camera video shared with the BBC showed confrontations between Israeli soldiers and border police and a large crowd of settlers. The security forces used tear gas and stun grenades.

In other footage, the Israeli forces appear to have confiscated the canopy under which the settlers were sheltering, while leaving their other equipment.

It is not clear exactly what the settlers in Qusra want. In the past, settlers have forced Palestinians out of their homes and seized their properties.

The stated aim of the settlers is to empty the area of its Palestinian residents.

Settlements are illegal under international law, but the Israeli government has promoted their recent rapid expansion.

The Palestinian village mayor, Abdel Azim Wadi, told the BBC that local residents had seen "a clear and sustained pattern of targeting Qusra". Last month a newly completed mosque was set on fire with graffiti in Hebrew sprayed nearby.

That settler attack was one of many that followed on from an incident in the Palestinian village of Tal. After Israeli settlers attacked Tal, it triggered an escalation in which six people were killed - four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers – one of whom acted as a security coordinator for a nearby Israeli settlement.

In July, settlers also surrounded a Palestinian home in the village of Jalud, near Qusra, for more than two weeks. Afterwards, the owners fled and settlers took over the property where they remain until now.

According to the UN's figures, 76 Palestinians – including 18 children - have been killed in the West Bank this year, by Israeli forces or settlers. At the same time, three Israelis – including one civilian – were killed in confrontations with Palestinians and in an alleged ramming attack by a Palestinian in the West Bank.

Since January 2023, 127 Palestinian communities in the West Bank have experienced full or partial displacement, including 47 that have been entirely displaced, affecting more than 6,390 Palestinians, the UN says.

It has registered that in 2026, about 3,800 Palestinians, nearly half of them children, have been displaced due to settler violence, demolitions and evictions.

Speaking at the UN meeting, Israel's Ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon dismissed the idea that settlements were an obstacle to peace. He said that they would remain and continue to grow as his country had biblical, historic and legal rights to the land.

He said that the Security Council "must understand a simple truth: we are not going anywhere".
